To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the feeding periodicities of benthic invertebrates vary widely and may be related to the availability and digestibility of food and the presence of predators, 2) the use of an electric shocker to collect benthic inverts does not affect their feeding periodicities, and 3) benthic inerts killed with certain preservaties may not be suitable for feeding studies.

1) the feeding periodicity of benthic invertebrates is not related to their body size, 2) the use of electric shocker for the collection of benthic animals is not justified, 3) animals collected by electric shocker are not suitable for grazing studies, 4) the use of preservatives for the collection of animals is not justified and 5) animals collected from the downstream river drift are not suitable for the analysis of gut contents.

1) the feeding periodicity of benthic invertebrates is largely controlled by the availability of food, 2) most animals collected by an electric shocker have empty guts, 3) the downstream drift of streams is composed largely of animals which have empty guts, and 4) animals killed by formaldehyde or by freezing have empty guts.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the feeding biology of the freshwater benthic invertebrates.
the feeding biology of the benthic macroinvertebrate fauna in a small, warm-water stream.
the feeding ecology of freshwater macroinvertebrates, particularly those species which feed upon the benthic algae.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
we do not know much about the feeding biology of the vast majority of the benthic animals.
the feeding biology of the benthic invertebrates is still largely unknown and that much work needs to be done before we can understand the feeding biology of these animals.
the feeding habits of benthic invertebrates are not yet well enough understood to be used in the management of streams.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the benthic fauna is capable of grazing large amounts of algae, that the grazing is not selective, that the grazing occurs in a periodic manner and that the grazing is more important in the early spring than at any other time of the year.

1) the methods used to study the feeding biology of invertebrates are not sufficiently accurate, 2) the results of experiments on the suitability of preservatives and on the periodicity of feeding of animals collected with an electric fish shocker are inconclusive and 3) the downstream drift of a river is not a reliable source for collecting invertebrates to use in feeding studies.

the benthic fauna of the River Thames are highly selective in their feeding, but that this is not necessarily a result of their having a wide choice of food, since the fauna is composed of a few dominant species which are highly selective in the food they consume.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we should be very wary of the conclusions drawn from feeding studies of benthic invertebrates, and that we need to develop new techniques to overcome some of the problems of error.

the methods used in collection and preservation, as well as the techniques of gut content and grazing studies, must be improved before we can hope to make any progress in our knowledge of the ecology and feeding biology of bethic invertebrates.
it is necessary to use a method of collection which will not alter the feeding periodicities or the gut contents of the animals being collected.
